The financial gap between the Premier League’s traditional Big Six and the rest of the division continues to widen, with new figures highlighting how England’s wealthiest clubs are strengthening their dominance through commercial revenue, broadcasting deals and increased spending power. Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea have established themselves as the league’s financial heavyweights, generating hundreds of millions of pounds more than their domestic rivals. A report by BBC Sport on Thursday highlights how the growing financial advantage is making it increasingly difficult for other Premier League clubs to compete with the established elite. The scale of the divide is reflected in the figures involving Everton, the only club outside the Big Six to have remained in the Premier League since its formation in 1992. In 2009-10, the average revenue gap between the Big Six and Everton stood at £120 million. By 2024-25, that figure had increased to £442 million. The growth has largely been driven by the expansion of international broadcasting rights and the commercial appeal of clubs with huge global fanbases. According to University of Liverpool football finance professor Kieran Maguire, the biggest clubs have become particularly attractive to international sponsors because of their worldwide following and the Premier League’s global television reach. The report revealed that commercial deals account for 45 per cent of the Big Six’s revenue, compared with just 10 per cent for Everton. Smaller clubs consequently depend more heavily on broadcasting income, which accounts for 66 per cent of Everton’s revenue. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. UEFA’s value pillar, introduced as part of its Champions League financial distribution system, reserves 35 per cent of competition revenue for clubs based on their historical performance and commercial value. This has further strengthened the financial position of established European giants, with Manchester City earning an estimated £37.9 million from the value pillar last season, compared with Newcastle United’s £13.6 million. Aston Villa and Newcastle have both improved their financial positions through European qualification, but the distribution system continues to favour clubs with stronger historical records. Meanwhile, Chelsea are beginning to fall behind their traditional rivals financially, with Stamford Bridge’s limited capacity identified as a major obstacle to increasing matchday revenue. Mudryk blames Ukraine national team for failed drug test Ince tells United to chase Watkins, Toney over Osimhen Bassey hands Devils boost as Fulham set huge price The report noted that Chelsea recorded the lowest revenue among the Big Six over the past two seasons, finishing £74 million behind Tottenham and £200 million below Liverpool and Manchester City. Despite generating an average of £80 per supporter in matchday spending during 2024-25, Chelsea’s 40,000-capacity stadium leaves them at a disadvantage against rivals whose grounds hold at least 60,000 spectators. Their matchday revenue has increased by only £16 million over the past decade, compared with £69 million for Manchester United and £85 million for Tottenham following the opening of their new stadium. The introduction of the Premier League’s squad-cost ratio (SCR) rules could further strengthen the spending advantage of wealthier clubs. Unlike the previous profit and sustainability rules, SCR allows clubs to spend a percentage of their revenue on squad costs, giving clubs with higher earnings greater financial flexibility in the transfer market. Although the new system offers clubs such as Aston Villa and Newcastle more room to invest, Maguire believes the structure still favours the Big Six because of their significantly greater revenue. The financial consequences are already becoming evident in the transfer market. Premier League clubs spent a record £3.5 billion during the summer transfer window, while 13 clubs broke their transfer records. Brentford, Brighton, Crystal Palace, Leeds United and Nottingham Forest were among the clubs to spend more than £40 million on individual players, highlighting how transfer spending is spreading across the division. However, the growing financial power of the biggest clubs means they remain better positioned to compete for elite players and offer more attractive wages. While clubs such as Brighton have demonstrated that intelligent recruitment, player development and effective financial management can challenge the established order, sustaining that success remains difficult. The report suggests that the Premier League’s financial structure is increasingly reinforcing the position of its wealthiest clubs, raising further questions about the long-term competitiveness of the division. The article is based on the BBC Sport report, with the financial figures and explanations retained. Deloitte’s latest figures also show that Premier League clubs generated £6.8bn collectively in 2024-25, with the Big Six accounting for almost three-quarters of commercial revenue.
